t: LOST between the {time} glide and the ring counter: a heliox flute in a grey felt bag, 1.2 metres long and hard to miss. Reward of a crock of black garlic. Ask for {name} at Ring {ring}.
FOUND in a cab from Core {n}: a child's left shoe, resoled at least twice, with a name in the heel worn past reading. It is at the {block} school office, being missed.
Lost on {street}: a tin of the Nine with my grandfather's dents in it. The Nine inside is ordinary. The tin is not. {name}, deck {deck}.
FOUND on the {block} stair, deck {ldeck}: a spool of hard algae blue thread, nearly full. Whoever is relining something in algae blue, it is pinned under this notice.
SWAP: our two rooms on deck {deck} for three rooms anywhere. The baby carries a share now, and has started to act like it. Ask for the {surname} household at the Court.
SWAP: our Hollow turn, {weekday} at lamp-dawn, for any turn after nine. Nobody at our table is awake at lamp-dawn and the lake is wasted on us.
WANTED: a cot, any age, any colour. Ours went to a cousin in {nb} and has not come back, which is how cots go.
WANTED: someone who can mend a cleaning robot that cleans only the left side of rooms. It is very thorough about the left. {name}, deck {deck}.
OFFERED: an armchair, 140 years old, sprung twice and covered three times. The present cover is mustard, and that is the only reason it is free. Collect from deck {hdeck}.
OFFERED to any young household: a full set of lids, eleven sizes, from my mother's kitchen. I eat at the hall now and they deserve a table. Ask for {full}, deck {hdeck}.
LESSONS: heliox flute for beginners. Your arms must reach the end of the flute; we will measure. {weekday} evenings, the back room of the {block} hall.
LESSONS in mending: darning, patching, letting out a seam. Bring the thing you have been meaning to throw away. You will not throw it away. {street}, {weekday} evenings.
The {block} choir is short of altos and long on opinions. New voices welcome on {weekday} after supper. The room is felted; you will sound better than you think.
WANTED: a recording of the old {block} brass band from before the hall was felted. It will sound as though it was played through a blanket. We want it anyway.
To whoever practises the bass flute on deck {deck} after the lamps fade: you have come on a great deal this year. Please come on somewhere else.
Spoons of my great-grandmother's rye starter, free. It is registered, it is sour, and it has outlived three of her crocks. Bring a clean jar to {name} at the {block} hall.
Crock clinic at the Gate, Ring {ring}, {weekday}: bring a sour one, a slow one or a sulking one. A Gate hand will sequence it and tell you, kindly, what has moved in.
The Gate at Ring {ring} reminds travellers that yogurt is alive. So are kefir, miso, cheese rinds, your grandmother's sourdough and the seeds in your pocket. Declare them. We are nice about it.
GATE: cultures held for checks may be collected from the cold room after seven days. One rye starter, unlabelled, has been with us since {weekday} and is getting ideas.
Will whoever left a jar of amazake by the 65 °C tap in the {block} baths please collect it. It has been warm for {n} days and has views.
Jars wanted, any size, with lids that close, for the {block} Knotnight larder. Bring them to the hall and take a jar of pickles away.
Lost: one black thread, off my left wrist, somewhere on {street}. If you find it, please do not message me. I won't see it. Tie it to this board.
FOUND at the ring counter, Ring {ring}: one glove, left hand, darned so often it is mostly darn. Behind the broth urn with the other lost gloves, which are also all left hands.
SWAP: one high-deck flat on deck {hdeck}, quiet, low dose, lovely light, for anything on a low deck near my grandchildren. I have been light long enough. Ask for {full}.
SWAP: wing-sleeves, remade, blue, cut for someone tall and patient, for a good pair of shoes. Mine are going and I have stopped flying. {name}, deck {deck}.
WANTED: a minder for two children, {weekday} afternoons, the usual rate. They are good children. One of them throws everything anti on purpose. The {surname} household, deck {ldeck}.
OFFERED: a hand lamp, two watts, mended twice, flies well. Free to anyone going up the Spindle who hasn't one. Ask {name} at the Ring {ring} counter.
LESSONS: spinball for grown-ups who were never picked. Axis flies true, spin sinks, anti floats; we start from there. The long hall, {weekday}. No shouting.
LESSONS in writing to someone far away: how to write a long letter that will still be true when it lands. {name}, {weekday} evenings, the {block} hall.
The {block} youth ensemble wants one more tenor shawm, and a parent willing to hear it at home.
The {block} quartet plays on {weekday} after dinner, in the felted room. Please keep your lids on until the slow movement. Last time a spoon rang for a full bar.
FOUND on the stair at deck {ldeck}: a child's spinball, very scuffed on one side. It was thrown anti and went a long way. Now at the {block} school office.
Will whoever borrowed the {block} hall's big stockpot for a wedding please bring it back. We know it was a lovely wedding. We can tell from the size of the gap on the shelf.
WANTED: someone to read aloud to my mother on deck {hdeck}, two afternoons a week. She was forty years on the back crews and likes books with very few people in them. Usual rate.
The {block} lending cupboard has a noodle press, two ladders, a hem press, a crib and a single wing-sleeve. If you have the other wing-sleeve, we would very much like to meet you.
LOST: my aunt's recipe for onsen custard, written on the back of a Booking Day menu. The custard is ordinary. The handwriting is hers. {name}, the {block} hall.
To whoever is growing coriander on the shared shelf at the end of {street}: thank you. To whoever is eating it: please stop at half.
OFFERED: felt offcuts sorted by colour, enough to hush one small room or two loud children. Free from {surname}'s on {street}.
WANTED: an old coat to be cut down for a wander year. Must have pockets, a lining and no strong opinions about colour. Will trade a crock of chilli crisp. {name}, deck {deck}.
SWAP: a crock of miso from our larder, two years down, for a jar of pickled plums. The plums are for a wedding. The miso is for you. The {surname} household, {street}.
FOUND in the {block} baths: a bath sheet embroidered NOT YOURS. It was right. Now at the desk.
LESSONS: the larder knots, for tying down jars. They have nothing to do with Knotnight, whatever your grandfather says. {block} Court, {weekday}.
The {block} baths close for cleaning on {weekday} from {time}. Steam resumes at noon. Gossip may continue in the corridor.
CLINIC: yearly dose checks for back crews and anyone who has signed for a guest shift behind the radiators. Bring your card. {weekday}, deck {ldeck}. Nothing hurts but the wait.
FOUND: one orchard apple, whole, on the floor of the lift lobby on deck {deck}. Somebody has lost a gift. It is in the clinic's cold drawer. Nobody has eaten it, though we have all looked at it.
WANTED: good paper, a quire or so, for deck {hdeck}. My grandfather is writing a long letter to a raft across the Shade and drafts by hand. It goes by light; the paper stays with us.
OFFERED: the use of my sewing machine on {weekday} evenings in return for company. I am ninety-one. I do not need help. I need someone to tell me about the new collars.
LOST between the Glide and home: my son's crew patch, a square with a band of stitched stars. It was his grandmother's. He is eight and not speaking to us. Ring {ring} or deck {ldeck}.
The lamp fade on {street} has been running eleven minutes late since {weekday}. The lamp office knows. The children also know, and are using it.
Will the household on deck {deck} that runs its laundry at seven in the evening please try one in the morning, like everyone else. The kays are cheaper and the walls are thin.
SWAP: a pair of shoes, nearly new, half a size wrong (the shop was right, I was not), for a pair half a size right. {name}, {street}.
WANTED: anyone who remembers the Eleven Days and will tell the {block} school's oldest class about it. Tea, a felted room and twenty-three very serious faces.
Choir master seeks a bass who can sing a low D in heliox without looking strained. The last bass looked strained. {block} hall, {weekday}.
The stairwell at deck {deck} rings for six seconds and the {block} brass quartet has noticed. Rehearsals on {weekday}. Doors may be shut on request.
STARTER SWAP at the {block} hall, {weekday}: bring a spoon, take a spoon. Labels compulsory. A Gate hand will be there to say which of you has brought a phage.
The strain library keeps a copy of every registered starter in the drum. It does not keep your grandmother's hands. Please feed your crock.
FOUND near the Hollow lake on {weekday}: a child's sandal, very wet. The lake is part of the water reserve and gets sieved, so it was always going to turn up. Cab pavilion desk.
The ring counter at Ring {ring} is out of rice balls until {time}. Broth continues. Arguments about the broth continue.
To the person who keeps correcting the spelling on this board: thank you. To the person correcting the corrections: there is a choir that needs you.
WANTED: two hours a week of someone patient with a lathe. Our grandmother's chair has lost a foot. The other three feet don't match either, so the bar is low. {name}, deck {deck}.
The {time} glide to {nb} is running. The Glide is always running. This notice is here because somebody asked.
Glide cars do not take hot soup. This now also applies to cold soup, after {weekday}'s incident on the {time} to {nb}.
LOST on the {time} glide from {nb}: a child's hat, which came off at the release and was last seen drifting toward the aft window. It is somewhere in car {n}.
To whoever sits in the aft seat of the {time} glide and names the quay lights out loud: we have learned them all now. Thank you. Please learn the next row.
SLOW CYCLER to {farrow}: boards by capsule at Ring {ring} on {weekday}. 1.1 kays and some weeks of soup in bulbs. Bring something from this drum for the Galley's stockpot.
To {far} by the slow line: 1.1 kays, and weeks of weightless soup. By the express: 111 kays, and days. The cycler office takes no side in this. The Galley does.
WANTED: a companion for the slow line to {farrow}, some weeks, no weight. I bring cards and a good starter. You bring the bungee hour, because I won't do it alone.
Back from the slow line: one pair of legs that has forgotten how to stand. Their owner thanks the {block} baths for the use of a rail, and promises to do the bungee hour next time.
Black garlic from the 65 °C loop, three months down, at the {block} hall counter. A quarter of a kay a jar. Lids back, please.
Onsen custards, warm from the waste-heat loop, at the {block} baths after {time}. They are wobbling as intended. Spoons on the honour shelf.
Three ripe tomatoes in the glass case at {surname}'s on {street}. Half a kay each. One is spoken for, for a wedding, and has been given the middle of the case.
Have some Nine. (The {block} clinic keeps this notice up all year. Somebody always looks peaky.)
Vintage night at the {block} hall: the blight menu from the year the cheese line failed, cooked as it was. The elders say it was worse. Bring your own salt.
This week's ring counter broth at Ring {ring} has a sprig of something nobody can name, and the crew won't say. Guesses on a slip, please. The winner gets a second rice ball.
To whoever lifted the lid off the stew at the {block} hall and left it off through the whole of the reading: we saw. Your aunts saw. The stew is cold, and so are we.

THE COURT'S LIGHT: the {block} vote is on {weekday}. Full brightness on the floor for the pears, or half over the whole Court for the terraces. The pears have won {n} times running. The pears do not vote.
OFFERED: a two-watt grow lamp, very old and very reliable, from a herb shelf that outlived its owner. It kept basil going for {years} years. It will keep yours.
The lamps on {street} will ramp up at 06:20 instead of 06:30 from {weekday}, at the bakers' request. Everyone else may keep their eyes shut for ten minutes.
To my neighbour on deck {deck}, who has lit their flat like lamp-noon for a month: we are happy for you. We can see it under the door. We are very happy for you under the door.

A long letter has landed for the {surname} family from a raft across the Shade, sent {n} years ago by an aunt who swapped away at a Passing. They will read it once, in the {block} hall, on {weekday}. All welcome. Nobody talk.
Cards home: the {block} post desk sends cards by light to any drum on Merrow and stamps each with the delay. Longest this month: forty-one seconds, to a grandmother on {farrow}.
WANTED: a fourth for a slow world, the forty-second kind. We plant orchards together across Merrow and our last gardener has moved to {far}, which is no excuse but is a reason.
MENDING at {surname}'s, {street}: linings in this season's hard algae blue, cuffs turned while you wait, children's trousers let out (the third time is the last time).
Shoes resoled in an hour. New shoes are twenty kays; mine are about four and a story. {name}, {street}, behind the clinic.
Cloth bank collection on {weekday}, the {street} bins: clothes past mending. Nothing is past mending, but some things are past wearing. The Yards will take them back to thread.
SPINBALL: {block} under-twelves against {nb}'s, the long hall, {weekday}. Their coach teaches them to throw anti. So does ours. It will be a long afternoon.
Elders' swimming at the Hollow lake on deck {hdeck}'s turn, from lamp-dawn. A dive at half a g takes long enough to change your mind halfway down. Please don't.
SPINBALL RESULT: {block} 4, {nb} 4. The deciding throw went spinward and dived into the referee's lap. Replay on {weekday}. The referee has asked to stand further back.
The back flying hall is closed on {weekday} for re-netting. The front hall stays open. Please fly lengthwise. Crosswise is why we are re-netting.
LOST in the flying hall: a wing-sleeve, left, olive, patched at the elbow. Without the right one it is a very dear scarf. Ask for {name} at the hall desk. Small reward.
The Spindle opens at lamp-night as usual. The lamp office reminds flyers that the sunline is a dark cable by then, and still not a handhold.
HOLLOW TURN: deck {deck} has the bright half on {weekday}, nine to three. The children of that deck have already told everyone in the lift core. Twice.
The Hollow's apples are not for picking. Each one is counted, wrapped and sold as a gift, and the woodwardens can tell. Please stop testing whether they can tell.
LOST from the elders' bench by the lake: a faded green cushion, sat on for {years} years by the same person, who would like it back. Leave it on the bench.
{full}, lift engineer for most of a century, has died at a great age. The cabs in Core {n} will stand still for one minute at noon on {weekday}.
{full} has died, aged a hundred and nine, on deck {hdeck}. The herb shelf will be shared out on {weekday}. Bring a pot and a story about the rosemary.
The family of {full} thank everyone who came to the hall. The stew was too salty because we were crying into it. It will be better at the naming.
NAMING: {name} {surname}, born on {weekday} into the share of {full}, who died last year on deck {hdeck}. The two families will eat together after. Please do not compare noses.
Every year we send a note to the family of {full}, of deck {hdeck}, whose share our {name} carries. This year our note came back. If you knew the family, please ask at the {block} hall.
WORK: the Gate at Ring {ring} needs a night hand. Steady hands, a good nose for yogurt, and the patience to tell someone their grandmother's culture must wait a week.
BACK CREW: the Ring {ring} crew is one hand short for the long rota. You must be able to hold a spanner, a conversation and your nerve. The view is famous. The pumps are not.
WORK: early cooks for the {block} Mill Hall jook. 05:30 start, warm kitchen, all the chilli crisp you can carry. Usual rate.
WORK: a mender for cleaning robots on {street}. Three of ours are lined up at the shop door and will not clean anything until they have been seen.
WINDOW: eight-year-olds on {weekday}'s list, bring your adult and a warm layer. Twenty minutes in the red light first, so your eyes wake up. Nobody wants to waste their one time.
Thank you to the back crew who took our class to the Window on {weekday}. Several of the children now refuse to sleep with a lamp on. Their parents would like a word.
The Vats have changed the yeast in the Mill lager this month. If you can taste the difference, they would like to hear from you, quietly.
Never drink spirit sold from a bag or from a bottle without a label. The food plant's methanol is not gin. This notice is up because it has to be.
LARDER CHECK before Knotnight, from the {block} block office: please look in your larder. If the hard bread could be used to wedge a door, it is time.
To the child who drew a five-pointed star on the lift doors at deck {ldeck}: it is very good. It is also on the lift doors. Please bring a cloth.
Booking Day menu at the {block} hall: cultivated steak with herb butter, a salad cut generously for once, and an apple between two. Seats by lot. Elders first, children last and loudest.
Thank you to whoever left herb cuttings at our door on deck {deck} after the funeral. The shiso has taken, which is more than we have yet.
The {block} school lends 2,500-lux light panels to anyone who keeps missing their morning twenty minutes. Sign one out at the office. The children will check on your posture.
{nb} has told us their ring counter broth is better than ours. We have tasted theirs. Our findings will be posted on {weekday}.
RE: the notice about our broth. It is meant to be that peppery. (The Ring {ring} counter staff.)
FOUND on deck {deck} at 01:10: a laundry net with one sock in it. The machines had the lamp-night and the sock took its chance.
WORK: night hand for the vat lines, Keel deck {n}. The vats turn over in the lamp-night and someone has to watch them do it. Quiet work, warm floor.
Will whoever taught the {block} children to use 'anti' as a verb please come forward. They have antied three cups and a teapot this week.
WANTED: a lid for a medium pot, any colour. Ours went antispinward off a terrace and has not been seen since. We are covering dinner with a plate, and the neighbours on deck {deck} have noticed.
The slow-line timetable has not changed in living memory. This notice is replaced every year anyway, because people like reading it.
LESSONS for nervous gliders: we sit you in a cradle on the quay and show you, slowly, what it feels like when your weight comes back. Then a car will do it in two seconds. Ring {ring}.
Quaysides market, Ring {ring}: cherry tomatoes from {nb}, strawberries from {nb2}, and for one day only a single melon from {far}. The melon is not for sale. It is for looking at.
SWAP: my {weekday} shift at the ring counter for any other day. I have joined a choir, and the choir cannot do without me, or so they say while I'm in the room.
LOST: a starter crock, yellow, chipped at the lip, and also my memory of where I put it down on {weekday}. Either would help. {name}, deck {deck}.
Slow-world evening at the {block} hall on {weekday}: games made for the forty-second wait, with friends across Merrow. Bring a cushion and patience. The tea is free.
The {block} reading room now stays open through the lamp-night, for those who can't sleep and those who have stopped trying. Felt on every wall. Whisper; it carries.
FOUND in the cab lobby on deck {deck}: a paper twist holding five dried apple seeds. Somebody kept the star. It is at the lobby desk.
OFFERED: room on my crock shelf for anyone leaving on a wander year with a starter to be minded. I feed weekly, talk to it daily, and hand it back with a full report. {name}, {street}.
WANTED: someone to teach my grandmother a slow world, so she can play cards with her sister on {farrow}. She says the wait between moves is the best part. We can't argue with that.
LOST on the platform at Ring {ring}: a heavy jacket. The pockets hold three spoons of starter in twists of paper and a note for the Gate. Please hand it to the Gate. They'll know.
Please mind the gap between the glide car and the quay. It has not changed in {years} years. Neither has this notice, apart from the number.
Spinball referee wanted for the {block} long hall, Saturday mornings. Must know the rules, enjoy being shouted at in heliox, and stand well clear of spinward throws.
Children's reel class on the third-g terrace, {weekday} after school. Every leap lands a hand's width spinward, so we will have gone once round the terrace by the end. Soft shoes.
New rule at the {block} baths: no reading in the steam room. The pages curl and so do the readers. Gossip is allowed, as always.
{full}, forty years at the Gate, retires on {weekday}. There will be cake at Ring {ring}. The cake has been sequenced.
Herb shelves repaired: grow lamps rewired, trays relined, basil given a talking-to. {surname}'s on {street}, mornings.
Please return the {block} Court's tall ladder. The pears need pruning, and the pruners cannot fly at nine-tenths of a g, whatever you've heard.
The {block} pears are in blossom. The youngest class brushes them on {weekday}. Adults may watch but may not help. Last year an adult helped.
PEARS: this year's first pear goes to {full}, oldest in the block. The second goes to the newest baby, who will not appreciate it. The rest by lottery on {weekday}.
Message for {name}: your aunt on {farrow} says the card arrived, the forty seconds were worth it, and please wear the coat.
WANTED for a school project: anyone who has seen the River and can describe it without saying 'gold'. The {block} school's oldest class has heard 'gold'.
There is a cup on the floor of the {block} hall that missed its saucer by two centimetres, antispinward. It has been left there as a lesson.
Lift core {n} closes for {n} days for a new gimbal. Please use the other cores. The stairs remain open to anyone who wants to eat breakfast twice.
OFFERED: a cradle that has rocked four of our family and is ready for one that isn't ours. Newly oiled, slight lean. Ask the {surname} household, deck {ldeck}.
To visitors: in this drum the lids come off at the table, not before. Watch your host. If they lift theirs, lift yours. If they don't, wait.
The Ring {ring} counter has been voted the best broth on {row} by the {row} Broth Society, which meets at that counter. This is not a conflict of interest.
WANTED: a felt hanging for the {block} hall ceiling. We have a cook who sings, and a ceiling that agrees with every note.
LOST: one hour of our Hollow turn, which I swapped to {name} for a crock of plum jam on condition that it was a good crock. It was not. I would like my hour back.
For the larder: hard bread to the old recipe. Keeps for a year, tests your teeth for two. {surname}'s bakery, {street}.
Please stop asking the Gate whether your seeds will grow. They will. That is the problem. Declare them.
KNOTNIGHT: lamps down in the {block} Court at seven. We make the larder together and eat whatever's fresh, as if a long dark were coming. It isn't. Practice is half the pride.
Gate tours for schools, Ring {ring}: watch a crate of strawberries from {nb} be sampled, sequenced and let in. Children may not sample the strawberries.
THE LEDGER, Ring {ring}, tonight. Places 200,000,000. People 194,206,000. Margin 5,794,000. Born today 4,431; died today 4,428. Guests on guest-right 402,117. Names on the next board.
LEDGER NAMES, Ring {ring}: {name} {surname}, born on {weekday}, carrying the share of {full}, who kept the lamps on {street} for sixty years. Welcome, {name}.

The Margin office at Ring {ring} lends first homes to young couples: two rooms, lent until a place frees in the family. Furnished with whatever the last couple left, which is usually a chair and a quarrel.
GUEST FLATS: {n} free tonight on deck {deck}, three nights each, sheets clean, herb shelf stocked. If you came in on the {time} glide, someone is already looking for you.
BLOCK COURT, {block}, {weekday} in the Court: the heating on {street}, the Hollow swap for the choir, and a complaint about a neighbour's flute. The neighbour will play in their own defence.
Block court ruling, {weekday}: the flute may continue until 21:00. The trombone may not continue at all. Both parties have been sent to the baths to calm down.
{full} of deck {deck} has been drawn by lot for this year's assembly. Please stop congratulating them. It is a year of meetings. Sympathy is also accepted.
THE QUIET, the day before Booking Day: no worlds, no messages. The {block} hall opens at lamp-dawn with tea and nothing to do but talk. Children may bring a board game.
This year's Booking Day question: an hour more of sunline, or a bigger hall fund. The {block} hall would like to remind you which of those feeds you.
A TABLE WANTED: a cheerful child of two needs one more aunt before the naming. Duties: birthdays, the odd crisis, being called aunt whatever you are. Ask the {surname} household.
To the four aunts of {name}: the naming has moved to {weekday}. Please talk to each other about gifts. Last time there were four blankets.
Our {name} carries the share of {full}, whose family brought a chair to the naming, remade, older than both families. Thank you. The child has already been sick on it.
The {block} hall cooks every night. Eating alone is allowed. So is being asked, gently, why you are eating alone.
VOLUNTEERS for the {block} hall: chopping, stirring, carrying lids. Nine of our eleven volunteers are over seventy, and they would like someone younger to carry the stockpot.
VISIBLE MENDING circle, {weekday}, {block} Court. Bring a coat with a story. You will go home with a coat with a slightly longer one.
Gold thread for showing mends is in at {surname}'s on {street}. Also a dull brown, for those who want their mends seen only by people who look.
HOMECOMING: the {block} wanderers are due on the {time} glide on {weekday}. Tables to the front. Hand lamps for everyone. Aunts, please do not cry until the doors open.
Leaving party for {name}'s wander year, {weekday}, the {block} hall. Packing so far: one crock, a good knife, a coat with too many pockets. Advice welcome; the aunts' kind goes on the right.
THE LONG FLIGHT: {block} flies together from the back terraces at 22:00. Wing-sleeves, a hand lamp, someone to fly beside. First-timers fly lengthwise or not at all.

WANTED: an adult to fly the Long Flight with two eleven-year-olds whose parents don't fly. You need sleeves, a hand lamp and the patience to be told you're doing it wrong. Ask the {surname} household.
REFUGE: the drum has opened Margin places this month for families from a dark drum on {farrow}. Coats, lids, crockery and company wanted at Ring {ring}. Especially company.
To our new neighbours on deck {deck}, who came a long way with very little: the {block} hall is yours any night, and nobody will ask you anything until you want them to.
Sending a long letter across the Shade? The {block} hall will read it aloud for you first, as a last check. It will be read once over there. Better to hear the mistakes here.
Hour swaps: an hour of anyone's time here is about six kays. The {block} board matches hours to hours if you'd rather keep your kays: cooking for mending, reading for haircuts.
GUEST-RIGHT: three nights, a Margin flat and a seat at any hall. Sign the book at Ring {ring}. On the fourth morning you are a visitor, and visitors wash up.
The lent flat on deck {deck} has stood empty since {weekday} and the Margin office says it is getting sad. Couples who want to marry, please apply in pairs.
The old Count board hangs in the Ledger hall at Ring {ring}, beside the Ledger. School visits on {weekday}. It is good for children to see the numbers we used to keep.
The Margin is not for children. It is for guests, refuge, first homes and the next bad year. This notice goes up every year after the vote and is not aimed at anyone.
Long-table rota, {block} hall: if your name is on the board twice, you are cooking twice. If your name is not on the board, you are washing up. There is no third column.
{painter} asks for quiet on the end-wall terraces during {weekday}'s dawn rehearsal. Rehearsals run in the lamp-night, on a model the size of a table. Please do not lean on the model.
{painter}'s dawn on {weekday} opens in the brown-violet the back crews call bruise. Terraces open at {time}. If you've never been to a Window, this is the nearest thing.
RE: {painter}'s dawn last week. Yes, it was too slow in the middle. The painter knows. The painter is already working on next year's.
The {block} heliox choir sings from the middle of the Spindle at midnight on the Long Flight. A voice carries a long way along the axis. That is the point.
Aunts of a child leaving on their wander year: the {block} hall will help you write the first letter. It is harder than it looks, and nobody has ever got it short.
The {block} block court thanks the {surname} household for giving its Hollow turn to the refuge families. It will come back to them, with interest, in pears.
BOOKING DAY: the Ledger is read at every ring at 08:30, and {block} meets at Ring {ring}. Bring a hand lamp, a child, and anyone who would like to see their name beside someone else's.
The Ledger shows {n} wanderers home this week, met at the ring by their tables with hand lamps. If you saw a crowd of crying aunts on the platform, that was why.
STUDIOS from the Margin: three free on deck {deck} for anyone making something. Painters, players, writers, woodwardens on leave. Apply with a piece of work, any size.
FIRST HOME LENT: {name} and {name2}, who marry on {weekday}, have been lent the Margin flat on deck {deck}. Their aunts have already been round with lids.
MARGIN VOTE: the assembly keeps the Margin as it is. A motion to spend some of it on births failed, as it does most years. Its sponsors have been asked to dinner.
Refuge welcome dinner at the {block} hall: our new neighbours will be seated with their new tables. Bring nothing but your name and one good question.
WANTED for refuge families: warm coats, lidded bowls, children's shoes in any size, and someone to walk the new children to the {block} school on their first morning.
The {block} mending circle altered forty coats for refuge households this week. Each has one new mend in gold, so whoever wears it knows somebody made it for them.
Childless lives are full lives. The {block} hall honours this year's long-service aunts on {weekday}: thirty-one of them, with two hundred and six nieces and nephews between them.
From the assembly by lot: the hall fund goes up, the sunline stays at six hours, and the members ask, unanimously, that the lift on {street} stop squeaking.
The Long Flight: lost hand lamps from last year are still at the Spindle desk. There are two hundred of them. Some of them are probably yours.
A GIFT OF A SHARE: {full} has adopted a young couple from outside the family as heirs. The couple do not know yet. They'll be told at the block court on {weekday}. Keep your faces straight.
Homecoming tea for the families of wanderers, {block} hall, {weekday}. Say how much you miss them now. Once they're back you'll have to pretend you didn't.
Every block court ends with one question: is anyone in the block alone tonight who doesn't want to be? Say a name, and a hall will set a place.
Reel night on the back terraces, {weekday}, at a third of a g. Every leap lands a hand's width spinward, and by midnight we're back where we started. That's the dance.
The {block} choir sings the leaving song at Ring {ring} as the capsule closes. If you are the one leaving, you don't have to sing. You won't be able to.
LEDGER CORRECTION: last night's board gave the newborn {name}, carrying the share of {full}, one letter too few. The family would like this known, loudly.
Tonight the Margin fell by {n} places, one for each person off the {time} glide from a dark drum. Please be at the ring to clap them in.
Tables: if you stood at a naming in {block} more than twenty years ago and have lost touch with the child, the hall keeps a list. They have not forgotten you.
WEDDING: {name} and {name2} marry young in the {block} Court on {weekday}, with a lent flat and no children planned until a share frees. Come anyway. There will be an apple.
Wanderers in {drum} on guest-right: every hall's long table has a guest end. Sit there if you're shy, in the middle if you're not. Either way someone will ask where you've been.
Booking Day vote result: hall fund, by four points. The block court thanks the losing side for their dawns, which they would have liked to see longer.
The {block} hall seats four hundred and feeds six hundred. Please eat, talk, and give up your seat to anyone with a lid in each hand.
CHOIR AUDITIONS, {block}: three sopranos wanted who can hold a note in a hall that rings for four seconds. Bring your own felt if you're nervous.
Round singing on the end-wall terraces, {weekday} at lamp-dusk. The echo comes back off the far bank nearly ten seconds late, so by our reckoning the far bank is the second voice.
{block} hall noise rules: talking at any volume, singing to the end of the second verse, banging lids never. Our ears are old and our lids are older.
LESSONS: noodle pulling on the third-g terrace, {weekday}. At a third of a g a strand hangs three times longer before it tears. Yours will still tear. That is what the first ten lessons are for.
The {block} hall school wants storytellers for the youngest class, aged eighty or over. Experience required: having lived. Paid at the hall rate, with dinner.
COOK WANTED for the Thursday table, {block} hall. Four hundred covers, eleven volunteers, and a pot that hasn't gone cold since the cook before last. Ask for {name}.
Hall quarrel settled: the {block} soup was too salty AND the cook was right. The block court thanks both sides, and the cook for not walking out.
Our hall is too loud. This is a complaint, and also a boast. More felt arrives on {weekday}.
The {block} choir sings the Passing round again on {weekday}: the one we sent to a passing raft, which came back sung against itself. Bring a handkerchief for the gap.
LOST at the Thursday hall, {block}: a long ladle, dented the year it stirred for four hundred and fell on a cook's foot. The cook would like it back. The foot has forgiven it.
SWAP: I will teach your child the long flute if you will teach mine to cook anything at all. The {surname} household, deck {deck}.
Supper and song at the {block} hall every night but the Quiet. On guest-right? Sit anywhere. From {nb}? Sit near the door. We are still cross about the broth.
THE BIG COOK for Booking Day: volunteers to the {block} hall from lamp-dawn. Four hundred steaks, two hundred apples to cut crosswise, and one person whose only job is lids.
WANTED: a quiet corner. We love the {block} hall and always will. If anyone has a room where nobody sings, please tell {name}. We'll bring cake.
RE: the quiet corner. There isn't one. Welcome to {drum}.
Hall musicians' rota: strings on {weekday}, voices every other night, and long flutes only when the hall is full enough to soak them up.
The {block} brass band has been asked to rehearse with the doors shut. The band would like it known that it was rehearsing with the doors shut. That was with the doors shut.
Please do not turn off the stockpot in the {block} hall kitchen to clean under it. Clean round it. Ask anyone why. They will tell you, for about an hour.
Story night at the {block} hall: {full} tells the Eleven Days, as heard from a grandmother who was nineteen at the time. The lamps go down for the second half.
LESSONS for adults: how to sing a round without winning it. {weekday}, the felted room. You'd be surprised how many people never learned.
You may change seats at the long table once a meal. You may not change seats to sit next to the cook. Everyone wants to sit next to the cook.
The table for eating alone has been taken out of the {block} hall. It was never used, and it was making the other tables feel guilty.
LOST: my voice, at the choir's all-night round on {weekday}. If found, it is high and a little thin, like everyone's. {name}.
The children of {block} have voted to call the {weekday} lunch 'second breakfast'. The hall has agreed. The menu has not changed.
THE HALL FUND at work: last year's vote paid for two more cooks in {block} and new felt for the ceiling. You can hear the difference. Some of you can hear it right now.
Our cook {name} is leaving us for {nb}, where the halls are smaller and, we're told, quieter. We will miss the dumplings. We will not miss the singing while folding them.
STRANGERS' NIGHT, {block} hall: every guest on guest-right gets a seat between two locals, who must ask where they've been. Locals, please practise listening.
LESSONS: lifting lids, passing plates and the order of serving at a long table, for wanderers who would rather not be the story at breakfast. {weekday}, five minutes, free.
TUTORS: the {block} hall school pays the hall rate, about six kays the hour. It also pays in dinner, which is the real reason anyone does it.
The {block} choir sings with {nb}'s on {weekday}, by link, a fraction of a millisecond apart. Neither choir can hear the gap. Both choirs say the other came in late.
Teaching hall timetable, {block}: reading in the mornings, sums at noon, cooking for anyone over six in the afternoons, and arguing, properly, on {weekday}.
WANTED: dishwashers for the late sitting at the {block} hall. The robots do the plates. People do the pans, because the pans have to be argued with.
SILENCE IN THE WOOD. Slates at the gate. In heliox a whisper carries a long way, so please don't whisper either.
LOST in the dim wood, near the third yew: a slate with half a sentence on it. If you find it, please don't finish it. {name} would like to.

WOODWARDEN wanted for the yew walk. A sixty-year post, more or less. The present woodwarden asks for someone who can be quiet for a whole shift and kind to birches. Apply in writing to the {block} lodge.
The {block} silent hall serves the Mill table at noon. Take a bowl, take a seat, taste the jook. If you want salt, point.
Chalk at the {street} stall: white, grey and the soft green everyone wants this year. Felt dusters. For the talkative we also stock very small slates.
Talking hour in the {block} Court, {weekday} from {time}: gossip, arguments, songs. Please get it all out. The wood is closed to voices afterwards.
Somebody left a slate on the lift doors at deck {deck}. It said THANK YOU. We don't know what for. It has been passed on.
The birches on the spinward slope are being thinned from {weekday}. If you hear a branch fall, that is us. If you hear us talking, something has gone wrong.
LESSONS: reading slates, lips and faces, for new arrivals from loud drums. Lesson one is how to stop saying 'sorry?' {weekday}, the reading room.
Silent flats on deck {hdeck} for guests on guest-right, three nights. You will hear the fans, the pumps, the water in the walls, and at last your own thoughts, which is the hard part.
To whoever whistled in the wood on {weekday}: it was lovely, and everyone within half a kilometre now has the tune stuck. Please don't.
CALLINGS: the woodwardens, the night readers and the copyists' hall take two new members each this year. Childless lives are full lives. Enquiries in writing, as you'd expect.
{full} sings alone at the edge of the wood every morning at lamp-dawn. By long agreement, this is allowed. Nobody has asked for it to stop in {years} years.
SLOW DOWN. The wood is the same size at any speed.
Planting day in the wood, {weekday}: each child plants one yew. It will be a tree when they are old, and a good tree when their grandchildren are. Spades provided. Talking is not.
WANTED: a slate with a crack in it, to replace mine. New slates have nothing to say.
The dim wood is lit to a quarter of lamp-noon, by choice of the assembly. Please keep hand lamps low under the yews. The yews were not consulted, but we think they agree.
SWAP: a bright flat on deck {deck} for any flat nearer the wood. I came here for the quiet and live over the Court's spinball pitch.
Please knock softly. The {block} reading room is next door, and the reading room hears everything.
The {block} silent hall thanks the visitor from {nb} who sneezed during supper. It is the hardest anyone in there has laughed in a year, and nobody made a sound.
LOST under the birches on {weekday}: an idea, about a third finished. If you picked it up, please finish it and leave me a slate saying how it ends. {name}.
Night walk in the wood with the woodwarden, lamp-night, {weekday}. Hand lamps on low. Three hours. You will hear the water in the walls. Some people cry; that is allowed.
OFFERED: twelve slates from a household that has gone back to talking. Mostly clean. One still says MILK in the corner and will not come off. Deck {deck}.
WANTED: a copyist for my mother's recipe book, before she forgets the last pages. She speaks rarely and writes beautifully. An hour a day at the hall rate. Ask for {name}.
The {block} viol consort plays the slow pieces on {weekday} in the felted room, at the volume of a conversation nobody is having.
The hour before the Quiet is the loudest hour in {drum}. Everyone has to say everything first. The halls open at {time} for it.
From the woodwardens: thank you for leaving the fallen yew where it lay. It will feed the wood for longer than any of us will walk in it.
For guests: carry a slate, eat the jook, walk slowly. If someone bows to you in the wood, bow back. You can ask what it meant afterwards, in the talking hour.
The {block} copyists' hall has finished copying the drum's oldest cookbook by hand. It was already copied perfectly a million times. This copy has a thumbprint in the gravy section.
Children of {block}: the wood's quiet is for the wood, not for you. Shout all you like in the long hall on {weekday}. We have hung extra felt.
RENTS RETURNED: this month's terrace rents have gone back into every wallet, about a fifth of a kay each. Spend it on something bright.
TONIGHT'S DUSK by {painter}: ninety minutes of rose and a long green end. Terrace seats by auction at Ring {ring}; standing room free. Rents back to everyone, as always.
The best seat on the end wall for {painter}'s dawn went for thirty-one kays, to a couple marrying there. Their table asks that nobody tell them what else thirty-one kays would buy.
The square on {street} is held at full lamp-noon for {n} hours a day, by vote. Wear something that looks good in it. Everyone else will.
LIGHT-PAINTERS' SCHOOL, {block}: three years for dawns, two more for dusks. Applicants must sit through one of {painter}'s dawns without once checking the time.
RE: {painter}'s green dusk. We accept that it was art. We would like the next one to have a little less of it.
WANTED: a shirt that looks good under a long lamp-noon. At least three owners old. The colour is up to you; the light will decide anyway. {name}, {street}.
The Ring {ring} arcade kitchen is cooking a soup that came by light from a raft across the Shade, dated by its light. Leave a recipe on the card; we send one back for every one we cook.
Dawn places are drawn by lot. The best terrace seats are auctioned, and every kay of rent comes back to every wallet. If that sounds odd, ask {nb} how theirs works.
Festival dressing on {street} begins {weekday}: coloured lamps, painted collars, dyed everything. Colour weighs nothing. Please don't hang anything heavy from the lift cores.
LOST on the terraces after the dusk: a shoe, which came off in a leap at a third of a g and landed a hand's width spinward of where anyone expected. {name}, Ring {ring} desk.
Please do not applaud the dawn before it is finished. {painter} has asked twice.
THE NOON VOTE: eight hours of full sunline, or seven and a festival of coloured dusks. Ballots at every ring. The painters have declared an interest.
Shop windows on {street}, festival theme: the River. Brown-violet strongly expected. The judges each saw the River once, at eight, and remember it differently.
This quarter the {block} terrace rents buy three more hours of Court light instead of coming back as a fifth of a kay each. Objections to the block court by {weekday}.
APPRENTICE wanted by {painter}: setting cues, timing dusks, and sitting on the end wall for six hours being told that wasn't it. Hall rate and your name on the dawn.
Every dusk is free from the Hollow floor. Only the terrace seats are auctioned. Visitors never seem to know this, so we have put it on a notice.
Festival week: the flying halls are lit from inside, in colour. Flyers, please do not hover in the red section. It is for the end.
Fashion in {drum} this season: linings in hard algae blue, collars in whatever colour {painter} ended the last dusk on. Mending and re-dyeing at {surname}'s, {street}.
Somebody has set the {block} lift lobby lamps to run a dawn every time the doors open. It is very good. The lamp office would like it to stop.
SWAP: two terrace seats for {painter}'s dusk on {weekday} for one seat at any dawn. We are early people married to late people.
The squares are for everyone, but they are bright. There are benches in the half-lit arcades off {street}, with water, and eye shades on loan.
Two painters have dawn and dusk on the same {weekday}. The lamp office has asked them to agree a colour for noon. They have not agreed a colour for noon.
Exhibition at the Ring {ring} arcade: costumes from forty years of festival dusks, each worn by at least six people. Touch the linings. That's where the stories are.
WANTED: someone who has never seen a painted dusk, to sit beside a young painter at their first. It helps them to watch a face instead of the sunline. Ring {ring} desk.
To visitors from {nb}: yes, our noon is longer. Yes, we pay for it together and the rents come back. No, we will not stop mentioning it.
The lamps on {street} have been painted gold for the festival. The paint weighs nine grams a lamp, and the lamp office would like you to say so to anyone who calls it waste.
THE DUSK CHOIR sings the last half-hour of every festival dusk from the end-wall terraces. New voices welcome. You must be able to hold a note while looking up. Rehearsals on {weekday}.
Thank you to the {block} children who held hand lamps along the end wall at the close of {painter}'s dusk. From the floor it looked like the whole raft's quay lights. It was one block's patience.
SPECTACLE COMMITTEE: volunteers needed to carry the long banner across the Hollow for the Booking Day noon. It weighs almost nothing at half a g, and still takes forty people. Sign up at Ring {ring}.
CRAFT SCHOOLS OPEN DAY, Ring {ring} workshops, {weekday}: chairs, flutes, sleeves and crocks. Watch a chair re-sprung in the time it takes to eat a bowl of noodles.
APPRENTICES wanted at the {block} chair school. Seven years, about a chair a year, and not one of them new. If you want to make new chairs, try another drum.
This quarter's fabrication allowance is in every maker's account: two kilos of new mass each. Spend it slowly. That is the whole craft.
The {block} workshop has three heliox flutes back from repair at 1.2 metres, and one at 1.4, which is either a mistake or a new instrument. Come and try it.
WANTED: an old chair, the worse the better, for a student's final piece. Must have at least three earlier repairs and one argument. {surname}'s chair school, {street}.
SLEEVE-CUTTING, {weekday}: we fit you, cut the fins, and send you up to the flying hall to see what you've done. Crosswise lessons after. The net is there for you.
Marrying someone from {drum}? Then you will be given one of the things we make. Please do not say you already have one.
TOOL LIBRARY, {block}: lathes by the hour, sewing machines by the day, the big press by appointment. Bring your own mass. We are a library, not a quarry.
To the student who made the six-legged stool: it stands. It also rocks on any heading you like. We are keeping it in the corridor of instructive mistakes.
LOST in the workshop: a brass thimble, flattened on one side, that came to me from my teacher and to her from hers. {name}, the {block} sewing school.
The {block} flute school will be tuning all day on {weekday}. Ear plugs at the desk, felt on the walls, and our apologies in advance.
Masters' rule in this workshop: show the mend. A hidden mend is a lie told to the next owner.
STARTER SCHOOL, {block}: a year with the crocks, learning to read a sour by smell. Your hands will be checked at the Gate before you touch a mother.
Visiting makers: guest-right here runs as long as you work. Teach a class, mend a thing, stay while you're useful. The {block} school will find you a bench.
To visitors: you are welcome to watch. You can't take one home today; the waiting list is longer than you are old. Put your grandchildren's names down.
WANTED: cloth offcuts heavier than shirting, for the sleeve school's practice fins. Students cut a great many wrong fins. It is how they learn the right one. To the {block} sleeve school, please.
The {block} lathe runs until {time} on {weekday}. It is a quiet lathe. The person using it is not.
CHAIR SCHOOL GRADUATION, {weekday}: every student's chair is remade from an old one, and each old one's history is read out. Sit in them afterwards. Please don't rock.
Fabricator hours: new mass by allowance only; remade mass any time. If you aren't sure which you are using, you are using new.
CROCK-MAKER wanted: good glaze, lids that seal, a lip that pours. Ours have dripped for two generations and we think that's long enough. Ask at {surname}'s.
A free sleeve fitting for any child under ten who can explain crosswise. Most of them can. Their parents mostly can't. The {block} sleeve school.
The varnish shop on {street} has moved to deck {deck} after {years} years. The smell has not moved yet. It will follow.
FROM THE MASTERS: we do not make things to last. We make things to be mended. It is a different skill, and it takes longer.
EXCHANGE: a term at our {block} school for a term at {nb}'s. Students only. Bring your tools. Bring them back.
LOST: my teacher's carving gouges, six, in a cloth roll mended more times than the gouges have been sharpened. {name}, the {block} school.
The {block} school gives one spoon of its old starter, registered and sequenced, to anyone who asks. Bring a label and a promise to feed it.
Students: the Gate has asked us to remind you that flute-cleaning brushes are not for the {block} pears. Not even at blossom.
MASTERCLASS: re-springing chairs with {full}, who has re-sprung more chairs than most people have sat in. Six places. Bring a cushion; you will be on a stool.
Please sort offcuts by fibre before the Yards collect on {weekday}. The Yards are polite about our sorting. They are not happy about it.
WORK: a finisher for the {block} flute school. You will spend your days making 1.2 metres of pipe sound like a voice. Steady hands, patient ears, hall rate.
HIGH-DECK ALLOTMENT: flats on deck {hdeck} go to the eldest on the list. {full} goes up on {weekday}. Come and wave; it is the last cab with all the chairs in it.
BIRTH RIGHT given: {full} gives a right, by deed, to a niece in {nb}. Witnesses at the registry on {weekday}. Thank-you cards to the giver, not the registry.
HOLLOW HOURS AUCTION, Ring {ring}, {weekday}: lake hours at dawn, terrace hours at dusk. The rents pay for the long noon. Bring your wallet and your patience.
Elders over ninety have the lake every morning at lamp-dawn. Everyone else, your turn is on the board. Please do not swim before you are ninety.
Visitors from {nb} may bring two bottles of gin each, duty free. Every visitor brings exactly two. The quay staff can count to two.
METHANOL WARNING: on {row} last year, four people died of spirit cut with the food plant's methanol. Buy gin from a licensed shop. If a bottle is cheap here, ask why.
{drum} keeps the guest-right compact. Wanderers may stay three nights in the guest rooms over the ring halls. Sign in at Ring {ring}. We have no Margin, so we keep a very good list.
SWAP: a flat on deck {deck} here for a flat in {nb}. My partner is from {nb} and misses the bright arcades. I miss nothing about them, but I am outnumbered.
{drum} finds {nb} dazzling and a little vulgar. {nb} finds us dim. Both drums are invited to the spinball final on {weekday}, where this will be settled.
At fourteen, half your dividend goes into your own name. Please do not spend it all at once on the express. Some of you are already looking at the express.
If your child is named for the person whose share they carry, the registry will give you that family's address for the yearly note. Most families are glad to hear.
Thank you to the {surname} household for this year's note on our father's anniversary. Your child sounds like a fine one. Our father would have liked the noise.
WINDOW: this drum's eight-year-olds go to the Window with one adult of their choosing. Next month's lists are up at the {block} clinic. Please don't take it personally if you weren't chosen.
Back crew pensioners' tea, deck {hdeck}, {weekday}. If you spent your working life behind the radiators, come and argue about which pump was worst.
WEDDING: {name} and {name2}, on the end-wall terrace at a third of a g, {weekday}. The apple will be cut at six. Gifts of Hollow hours to the couple's block office, please.
OFFERED: our grandparents' sofa, remade for our wedding, now too big for the flat we've swapped into. It needs another couple. It is good at weddings. Deck {deck}.
{nb} is brighter, our gin is cheaper, and the Glide is free both ways. If you're cross with us, try them for a week. Most people come back for the broth.
HOLLOW OFFICE: deck turns have moved by one week. If you have planned a picnic, you have planned it for somebody else.
Our gin is sold near cost, with thiamine, like the salt. We know {nb} taxes theirs. We know you take two bottles over. We know they know.
{full} has gone up. The shop on {street} is closed until {name} learns where everything is, which may take some time.
Cab help for elders from Core {n} up to the high decks after the Hollow turn. You will feel lighter when you get home. That is the deck, not your age.
Booking Day hall seats: elders by age, then everyone else by lot. If you are ninety and someone is in your seat, they are about to learn something.
The assembly has voted another hour of full sunline. The terraces thank you. The night flyers would like their hour back.
RE: the extra hour of noon. It is not showing off. It is one more hour of seeing the far bank clearly, which some of us like. (The lamp office.)
WANTED: someone in {nb2} who still has their grandmother's yogurt. Ours has gone thin, and the library's copy is the same yogurt, they say. It isn't.
Thank you to the Gate night crew at Ring {ring} for curing my wife's yogurt and giving it back. It is hers again. I eat some every morning and tell her the news.
LIGHT POOL: six households on {street} are pooling light for one shared garden wall, twelve hours a day. One more household and we can grow tomatoes. Ask {name}.
The {block} Mill Hall knows that everybody over thirty eats here by choice. It has seen you. It doesn't mind. Have some Nine.
The blight anniversary dinner at the {block} hall: the old vintage menu, the steaks that came out the wrong colour, tasting of nuts. Better than you remember, if you weren't born yet.
Hollow hours make the best wedding gift, and the auction is on {weekday}. Bid early. The couples on deck {hdeck} have already bid on each other's.
The new brass in the deck {hdeck} lift lobby was paid for by the residents, not the drum. The drum would not have chosen brass.
REGISTRY: the share of {full}, who died on {weekday}, returns to the pool. The child born into it will be named on the board. The family may send a note to the child, if they wish.
To the {surname} household on deck {deck}: our child, who is named for your mother, said a whole sentence today. We thought you would want to know.
The {block} Court's pears are in their tents for six weeks of winter. Please do not open the tents to check on them. They are fine. They are pears.
LOST: a Hollow slip for deck {deck}'s turn on {weekday}. Without it you'll still get in; you'll just have to argue. Please return it to the cab pavilion.
SWAP: a grey dress, re-dyed green for a wedding in {nb}, worn once, for anything in a colour they actually wear in {nb}. Apparently not this one.
EXPRESS SAVERS, {block}: teenagers going dark to save for the express to a friend across the raft. We meet in the baths on {weekday}, threads on, and talk about anything but worlds.
A fall on a high deck carries half the energy of a fall at the rim. It is still a fall. Rails fitted free on request on any deck above 301.
Grown-ups who missed the Window at eight: the back crew will take a party of twelve adults on {weekday}. It is never too late. It is only a little embarrassing.
{full}, forty-one years on the back crews, gave the crew patch to a grandchild at the Window on {weekday}. The crew asks that the grandchild keep it out of the wash.
WEDDING MENDING: your grandfather's coat relined in the colour everyone is wearing this year, about five kays of cloth and two hours of work. {surname}'s, {street}.
SWAP: our picnic places on the lake lawn for anyone's Spindle hour. My son wants to fly and I want to sit down. {name}, deck {deck}.
The vote on the gin duty is on {weekday}. For: fewer funerals. Against: more bootleggers. Arguments over: never, apparently.
Quaysides, Ring {ring}: produce in from {nb}. Cherry tomatoes, strawberries, and a crate of something round that the Gate is still thinking about.
The list for the high decks is up. If you are on it, congratulations on being old. If you are not, congratulations on being young.
To the visitor from {nb} who said our arcades were dim: they are. We like them dim. We can see you perfectly well.
WEDDING LISTS at the mending shop on {street}: couples list the old things they'd like remade, and guests each pay for an hour. A sofa is about forty hours. Please coordinate.
ENGAGED: {name} of {drum} and {name2} of {nb}. Both families are delighted, and each expects the couple to live in their drum. The couple have not said.
Thanks from {name} and {name2} to every guest who brought two bottles from {nb2}. We now have more gin than any household should. Please come and help.
The {block} school has won the {row} spinball cup for the first time in {years} years. The cup is felt-lined so that it doesn't ring. We have been ringing it anyway.
A birth right may be given to anyone you choose in this drum. Ask at the registry. It is the grandest gift there is, and there is no form for saying thank you.
BOOKING DAY: the beam is booked flat again. Harvest supper in every hall at six. Bring the oldest jar in your larder. Its time has come.
The fast line to {far} leaves Ring {ring} every {weekday}. 111 kays. If you went dark long enough to pay for it, you've earned it. Take the thread off once you've boarded.
Hollow hours here go by age, and the old go first. If you're young and cross, remember you'll be old. If you're old and pleased, remember you were young and cross.
You may pass any Hollow hour you're given to a family with small children. You'll get nothing for it. You'll feel wonderful.
Tea for people who don't glide: deck {hdeck}, {weekday}. Somebody who glided in that morning will bring the news from {nb}, and a bun.
REGISTRY: birth rights may be sold only through the registry, never in the arcade. If someone on {street} offers you one, it is not real and they are not nice.
Visitors from dimmer drums (we mean you, {nb}): our noon runs twelve hours, and the Hollow office suggests eye shades for your first. Yes, every visitor. Yes, even you.
OFFERED: two Hollow hours on the lake lawn, as a gift to any couple marrying this month. We married on somebody's hours forty years ago, and it is our turn. The {surname} household.
SWAP: our Low-deck flat near the school, deck {ldeck}, for one up in the middle decks, now that our youngest's bones are, we're told, finished.
The school pitch on deck {ldeck} is at nearly full weight, so throws dive harder there than anywhere else in {drum}. Kneepads are not optional. Neither is lunch.
Notes to the families of the dead go out with the post desk this week. If you've lost the address, the registry has it. If you've lost the words, the post desk has a few.
The bootleg spirit seized at Ring {ring} last month has been destroyed. If you bought any, please come to the clinic. Nobody will ask where from.
RETIRED: {full} has moved up to deck {hdeck} after a lifetime at the Mill Hall. Visitors welcome, especially with stew under a lid.
Wedding clothes, altered, at {surname}'s on {street}. Every dress here has been to at least four weddings. We will tell you which, if you ask.
The {block} Mill Hall jook now comes with chilli crisp on the side, at the request of the under-tens, who have been asking since they could talk.
WANTED: a minder for my mother, two hours on {weekday}. She is ninety-eight, lives on deck {hdeck}, and would like someone to argue with about the long noon.
The levy pays the Gate, the clinics and the back crews. Every year this notice goes up, and every year someone writes 'and the broth?' on it. Yes. And the broth.
To our neighbours in {nb}: thank you for the strawberries. Our Gate checked one in fifty, as usual. Our children checked the other forty-nine.
The Window gallery needs guides for the eight-year-olds' runs. Ex-back crew preferred: the children ask what it was like out there, and 'cold' is not enough.
SWAP: one bed, nights, for one bed, days. I work the vats through the lamp-night and my bed is empty all day. Yours, I hear, is empty all night. Deck {deck}.
WANTED: a room for one quiet lodger. Will mend anything in the flat and cook twice a week. Sleeps small. Snores, but in heliox it is high and brief. Ask for {name}.
Household of seven on four places seeks household of three on four places, for a long conversation about floor.
The {block} office thanks everyone for their patience in the cab queues at {time}. There are more of us than the cores were cut for, and there won't be fewer soon.
FOLD-DOWN BEDS remade from old tables at {surname}'s on {street}. Your table by day, your bed by night, your argument at both.
Deck {deck}'s Hollow turn now comes round every ten weeks. If yours falls on the day of a wedding, please swap it to the couple. Weddings first.

NAMING: {name}, a third child, born on {weekday} on thin shares, welcomed by four grandparents and the fourteen people who share their kitchen. Gifts of floor space gratefully refused. There isn't any.
THIN SHARES: the {block} Mill Hall serves second helpings to anyone on a thin share, no questions asked. The hall knows what a thin share is. Most of the hall is on one.
We're swapping our places to {nb}, where there is floor. If you need a cot, a pram or a table that seats eleven, come and take them. We won't need them there.
The block court reminds residents that cupboards are not bedrooms, however well felted. The clinic asked us to say so after {weekday}.
The {block} baths now run all through the lamp-night. If there's no room in your flat to sit, there is room in the water. It's warm and it's free.
SHARED KITCHEN, deck {deck}: breakfast in three sittings, dinner in four. Cook in another household's sitting and you feed that household. That is the rule, and it is why we eat well.
LODGER WANTED for a household with one spare corner. The corner has a lamp, a hook and a view of the kitchen. The kitchen is very interesting. Deck {deck}.
To new arrivals: in {drum} we say 'excuse me' twice, once going past and once coming back. There are a lot of us.
SPACE FOR HOURS: the {block} office keeps a list of households who'd give up a room for help. Mend, cook, read to an elder, mind a child. Rooms here change hands for hours, not kays.
WANTED: a cot that folds flat against a wall, in a flat that more or less folds flat against another flat. Deck {deck}.
If your household has started eating its larder, tell the {block} office. Nobody will shame you. Somebody will bring jars.
Day sleepers: the {block} clinic has dark cloths and ear plugs, free. Take two. Your neighbours are not getting any quieter.
Our elders on thin shares can't all go up; the high decks are full. If you have a room on deck {hdeck} and a soft heart, the {block} elders' table would like a word.
From the block court: no, we cannot vote ourselves more floor. We tried. The floor didn't come. Next item: the Court's light.
{name} and {name2} thank their whole block for the wedding: four hundred guests in a hall built for two hundred. Nobody fell over. Several leaned.
In {drum} the Mill table is the commons, and also the dining room, the study hall and, after nine, the dance floor. Lids on, please.
SWAP: half a wardrobe for half a bookshelf. The other halves are spoken for.
WANTED: a household that eats early, to share a table with a household that eats late. Same chairs, two sittings, twice the conversation. Deck {deck}.
The {block} school runs in two halves. Morning children, please leave the room as you found it. Afternoon children, please stop leaving notes in the desks. (Do keep leaving the notes.)
WANTED: someone with a gift for timetables. Nine households share one bath on deck {deck} and the rota has become a slow world.
A third child is a joy and the shares are thin. The {block} aunts' circle will help with minding, sleep and the hard months. You don't have to live in an open drum to be kind.
There is room in the Hollow for only a sliver of {drum} at once. Please be kind at the cab pavilion. The people behind you are not the reason.
SWAP: my turn in the quiet room for your turn in the bath. I need to think, and you need to stop thinking. Deck {deck}.
FROM THE HOUSEHOLD COUNCIL: {drum} has more people than places, by choice, by love and by accident. We are not counting. We are coping, and mostly cheerfully.
SWAP: a top bunk for a bottom bunk, any condition. I have slept nearer the ceiling than the floor for {years} years and would like to try the other one.
We're moving to {nb}: three places swapped for three over there, where the floor is wider and the broth is worse. We'll miss you. We won't miss the stairs at {time}.
Belongings may not be stored in the lift lobbies. Neither may grandparents, however much they like the company.
The {block} hall now has a quiet table by the wall, for anyone who hasn't had a minute alone all week. Eat slowly. Nobody will join you unless you nod.
LOST, in a flat of eleven: one hairbrush. If found, it belongs to whichever of us is shouting.
The {block} hall cooks double on {weekday} for any household that has had a death and a birth in the same month. We know what that month is like. We'll bring the pot.
To grown children still living at home: you are not a failure, you are waiting for a place. The {block} lodging list has households who'd swap a room for an hour a day. Apply in person.
The {block} block court has agreed two dinners a week in the Court, for everyone. Bring a chair if you have one. Bring a cousin if you don't.
Lift lobby chairs are for waiting, not sleeping. Unless you are very tired. Then they are for sleeping, and someone will wake you for your cab.
WANTED: a household leaving {drum} who'd leave us their herb shelf. We have no room for a shelf, but we have a wall that would hold one if we took the door off.
THE COUNT, Ring {ring}: places 200,000,000. People 214,900,000. Births licensed this year 450,000; deaths about 1,800,000. Par in about eleven years. Bets on the date may be taken off the platform.
The Count fell by 1,340,000 this year. The registry thanks everyone, and most of all the people who wanted children and waited.
FITTING DAY at the {block} clinic, {weekday}: fourteen-year-olds and their families at {time}, please. It is a small thing at the clinic and a big dinner after. Bring the family recipe.
LICENCE LOTTERY results are posted at the registry, deck {deck}. First children first. If your name is not there this year, the counsellors next door have tea and time.
Half the classrooms at the deck {ldeck} school are empty this year, so the elders' afternoon class has moved in. Please don't say anything sad to the elders. They are enjoying it.
The Count is an emergency measure with an end date, and the end date is par. The full statement is posted at every ring. It is short, and it has not changed.
PAR SWEEPSTAKE, {block}: guess the day the Count meets places. The closest guess wins dinner for two at the ring counter. The dinner is free anyway. The honour is not.
From the registry: the right of the Glide holds in {drum}. Anyone may glide out on any day. The registry would like to hear why, if you'd like to say. You needn't.
SWAP OFFICE, Ring {ring}, {weekday}: households leaving {drum} to raise children elsewhere, and households from {nb} who'd like a quieter drum. Biscuits provided.
To {name} and {name2}, who drew a licence in this year's lottery: congratulations from the whole of deck {deck}. We'll stop asking about names once you've chosen one.
Births at the {block} clinic this year: {n}. Each one is the whole block's. Welcome, all of you.
The {block} children's choir has eleven members under twelve. It used to have forty. All ages welcome now. We are especially short of altos who can still sing high.
From the council: we know the Count is hard and we know who carries it. The lottery is the fairest way we have found. When the Count meets places, the board comes down.
The old Count board from this drum's last stop hangs in the registry hall. This one will hang beside it, one day. The registry is already measuring the wall.
Fitting dinner at the {block} hall for this year's fourteens: {n} families, one long table. Speeches limited to two minutes. Aunts limited to one speech each.
Couples holding a licence may book the removal at the {block} clinic. Bring your licence and each other.
Visitors from open drums: yes, we count. Yes, it is the fitting at fourteen. No, we don't like it either. Please eat at the ring counter, and be kind about the broth.
Our blight menu outlasted the blight. The {block} kitchen still cooks it on {weekday}: puffed starch steak, mock apple pie. We'll stop when we reach par. Probably not even then.
The council is sending {n} observers to {nb} for their Booking Day, to watch their Ledger read. Residents may apply to go too. Bring a notebook and your manners.
Couples who drew no licence again: the clinic waiting room has been repainted, and the counsellors have been asked to stop saying 'next year'.
From this year the registry reads each licensed birth beside the name of the dead whose share the child will carry, the way the open drums do. We like it. We should have done it sooner.
The registry does not exist to judge. It exists to count. If you have a question about a pregnancy, the clinic is the place, and the clinic is on your side.
Proofreading is free for every child born in {drum}. Every child. The registry repeats this because people don't believe it.
THE COUNT, Ring {ring}: places 200,000,000. People 203,100,000. Par in a little over two years. The council asks that nobody start the party early. The council has already ordered the lids.
With so few children this year, every child in {drum} gets the bright half in the Hollow every week. Parents, please let them go. They'll remember it.
Grandparents without grandchildren: the {block} reading circle meets on {weekday} at the school, where there is room. Bring the book you would have read to them.
The Count is posted at every platform by law. The council has asked that it be lit no brighter than the timetable. It is a number, not a sermon.
THE FITTING: removable, painless, over in a quarter of an hour. The dinner afterwards takes longer. Questions to the {block} clinic from anyone, of any age, at any time.
Licence holders have {n} years to use a licence before it goes back to the lottery. The registry will send a polite reminder. Then a less polite one.
Newborns in {block} this year: one. The whole block is invited to the naming of {name} on {weekday}. Please don't all bring a blanket.
SWAP: our flat by the half-empty school on deck {ldeck} for one near a busy school. We hold a licence, and we'd like our child to hear other children.
The council's statement on the lottery: nobody is exempt. Councillors' names go into the same drum as everyone's, and are posted with the results.
Fourteen next month? The {block} clinic runs one talk for you and another for your parents. The one for your parents is longer. Tea at both.
THE COUNT dropped below 205,000,000 this week. There is a cake at Ring {ring}. It is not a big cake. It is a step.

For couples with no licence this year: the {block} clinic is open any evening. So is the aunts' table at the hall. None of us have children either, and we'd like to talk about something else for an hour.
Some families buy a birth right in a drum that sells them and place the child there. A licence from {drum} cannot be bought, and a child placed elsewhere grows up elsewhere. Think about the visiting.
The millions wheel on the Count board at Ring {ring} stuck this week. It only turns once a year and the hinge was dry. The registry apologises for a number nobody wanted to see stay put.
Welcome to the {n} households who swapped into {block} this year from other drums, for the quiet, the floor and the room in the Hollow. Come to dinner. We'll tell you about the Count.
The Count is not a punishment and was never meant to be one. If anyone treats you as though it is, the {block} court wants to hear about it.
Gate notice, Ring {ring}: produce from {nb} is through and on sale. They send it every week, and they never mention the Count. We are grateful for both.
Low-deck schools need fewer teachers, so the {block} school has three to spare for adult classes: sums, singing, and how to fix a cleaning robot.

The registry is open on {weekday} for questions about the register of places and shares, heirs, swaps and licences. The registry is not open for questions about when. Nobody knows when. Par knows when.
{full}, who mended half the coats on {street} and never once a coat of their own, has died. The coat is on the shop hook. Anyone who wants to add a mend, may.
Remembering {full}, back crew, who saw the River on ordinary working days for forty years and never tired of it. Tea in the {block} hall on {weekday}.
In memory of {full}, who taught the {block} children to throw anti for {years} years. The long hall will be quiet on {weekday} for the length of one game.
{full} has died at a hundred and twelve, the last in {block} who remembered the hall before the felt. The felt comes down for one evening, so we can all hear what it was like.
Tonight the Ledger reads {full} among the dead and, beside that name, a child called {name}. The two families will meet at the naming. The block court sends its love to both.
FOUND on the {time} glide from {nb}: a long letter, printed, folded small, half read. It is not ours to finish. Ring {ring} desk.
FOUND in the flying hall nets: one shoe, one spoon, a hairpin, and a hand lamp still lit. The nets catch everything that tries crosswise. Spindle desk, {weekday}.
FOUND outside the Gate at Ring {ring}: a small crock, unlabelled, very much alive. The Gate has taken it in. It is being fed, sequenced and, frankly, admired.
Our starter is older than anyone at our table and has been through four kitchens, two blights and one very bad wedding. It goes to {name}'s new household on {weekday}. Come and see it off.
Wanderers bound for Spelt on Grain Row: take a spoon of the {block} hall sourdough for Pell's crock room, so that {drum} is in this year's raft loaf. Jars at the counter.
If you sang through the whole 140 weightless seconds of the {time} to {nb2} on {weekday}, the catch crew at the far end would like a word, and an encore.
Children gliding alone must be met at the far quay. Write the name of whoever is meeting them on the label. 'Gran' is not enough. Every quay is full of grans.
The next Passing is due in about {n} years. The {block} choir has started learning songs to send, and the kitchen has started a list. It is never too early to get ready for strangers.
LEDGER, Ring {ring}: guests on guest-right tonight, 411,204. Wanderers, your aunts at home are reading their own Ledger and counting you. Please send a card.
